summary: Defines the policy for using 233/8 for statically assigned multicast addresses. It is a Best Current Practice.

plainLanguage.summary: It sets rules on how to get your own group-mailing addresses from a special block.

subtitle: How every network with an AS number gets its own block of fixed multicast addresses, with no sign-up step.

tldr.problem: Multicast group addresses were handed out by dynamic mechanisms, but many deployments, such as content aggregators, need addresses that stay fixed for long periods, and there was no agreed allocation scheme.
tldr.mechanism: The 233/8 block is divided by Autonomous System number: the first octet is 233, the next 16 bits are the AS number, and the last octet is local, which gives each AS a single /24.
tldr.outcome: Each provider gets a /24 automatically from the AS number it already has, but the scheme works only for two-octet AS numbers. It obsoletes RFC 2770.

facts.label: Layout
facts.value: 233, then 16-bit AS number, then 8 local bits

today: RFC 3180 is a Best Current Practice (BCP 53) and obsoletes RFC 2770. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why Fixed Multicast Addresses
sections.content:
RFC 3180 sets the policy for using 233/8 for statically assigned multicast addresses. The authors expect the space to be used mainly by many-to-many applications, in addition to the ranges already described by IANA, such as the administratively scoped ones in RFC 2365.

Multicast addresses had traditionally been allocated dynamically, for example with the Session Announcement Protocol (RFC 2974). The RFC says that many deployment models do not suit this: content aggregators need group addresses that are fixed on a time scale dynamic allocation does not offer, and providers, aggregators and application writers had no consensus on one allocation mechanism. The MALLOC working group had defined a global strategy (RFC 2730, RFC 2909), but it had not been widely implemented or deployed. This document addresses a subset of the problem: the cases not covered by Source Specific Multicast.
sections.plainLanguage: Some groups need a mailbox address that stays the same for a long time, and the old way of handing out addresses on the fly did not work for them. This gives them a steady address instead.

sections.title: Address Layout and Allocation
sections.content:
The scheme follows the case 1 allocation of RFC 1797, modified as follows. The high-order octet is 233, and the next 16 bits are a previously assigned Autonomous System (AS) number, as registered by a network registry and listed in the RWhois database system. The remaining 8 bits are local. That allows a single /24 per AS.

Because the AS number is used directly, each service provider gets a /24 automatically and no additional registration step is needed.

For example, AS 5662 is 0001011000011110 in binary, left padded with zeros. The high-order octet becomes the second octet of the address and the low-order octet becomes the third, giving 233.22.30/24. The part of 233/8 that maps to the private AS space (RFC 1930) is assigned to the IRRs (RFC 3138).
sections.plainLanguage: Your network's number is turned into part of the address, like a school number becoming the street name. So everyone can work out their own street without asking.

sections.title: The Two-Octet AS Limit
sections.content: The RFC states that this approach works only for two-octet AS numbers. In particular, it does not work for any AS number extension scheme, because there are only 16 bits in the address to hold the AS number.
sections.plainLanguage: The street name only has room for a short number. A school with a much longer number would not fit on the sign.

sections.title: Security and IANA Notes
sections.content:
The RFC says the approach may reduce exposure to denial-of-service attacks that are based on dynamic allocation. Since dynamic assignment does not cross domain boundaries here, well-known intra-domain security techniques can be applied.

For IANA, the document records that IANA has assigned 233/8 for this purpose. It replaces the earlier description in RFC 2770, which RFC 3180 obsoletes.
sections.plainLanguage: Because each network only hands out addresses inside its own street, it is easier to guard against troublemakers.
